The Working Response and Weights of One Equation

Source: R/coord.R
coord_working.Rd

Computes the working weights \(h_i\) and the working response \(z_i = \eta_i + s_i/h_i\), which define the weighted least squares problem that locally represents the log-likelihood.

Usage

coord_working(spec, ep, coef, design, p, expected, emethod)

Arguments

spec

A StatmodSpec().

ep

The linear predictors and the parameters that they imply, as statmod_eta() returns them.

coef

A named list of coefficient vectors.

design

The design.

p

Which distribution parameter's equation, a string.

expected

TRUE for the expected information, FALSE for the observed one.

emethod

The method that obtains the expected information: NULL (the closed form of the family where it has one, and distributions7::expect_opg() otherwise) or an object that inherits from distributions7::ExpectMethod. It is read only where the expected information is used.

Value

A list with w and z, each a numeric vector of length spec@n_obs. A row of weight zero has w zero and z equal to its predictor. The value is NULL where the working problem is not usable: a non-finite or non-positive \(h_i\), or a non-finite score, on a row of positive weight. The observed information can produce non-positive values far from the optimum.

Details

For a Gaussian response on the identity link the quadratic is exact and the first iteration solves the problem. Elsewhere it is the local approximation on which a scoring step works, and the weights are rebuilt at each iteration. A row of weight zero has no curvature and no score, and it enters the descent with weight zero at its own predictor.

Where the design carries a structural term, the predictor of an equation includes a part that belongs to that term, and the columns of a block do not carry it. The working response is then built on the static predictor, with \(s_i\) the score of the model from statmod_score_obs(), so the quadratic has the gradient of the log-likelihood at the current coefficients. The weights stay the family's curvature at the whole predictor. Another positive weight would change the path of the descent and would leave its fixed point where it is.
